prime.problem: Finding a key by scanning is O(n) per lookup. And some questions are about closeness, not equality (is any recent value within 3 of this one?), which an exact-match set can't answer without probing every value in the range.
prime.fits: The third Foundations card. It explains the O(1) average that the toolkit table promised for dict and set, then reuses the same idea with a bucket id you choose. The sliding-window cards and the composites later all lean on these dict lookups.
expect: hash → bucket, collisions, load factor, resize
what dict and set promise, and hashability
value buckets of width t + 1 for Contains Duplicate III
a window of the last k values
prime.goal: Explain why a hash lookup is O(1) on average and when it isn't, and solve Contains Duplicate III in O(n) by bucketing values so that one bucket and its two neighbours are the only candidates.

attend: Why does the load factor, not the number of keys, decide how long a lookup takes?
Why must the bucket width be valueDiff + 1 and not valueDiff?
Why is it enough to check your own bucket and its two neighbours, and never buckets two apart?
Why can each value bucket hold at most one value at a time?
What does floor division do for negative values that int(x / w) would get wrong?

must: Hash the key → pick one bucket out of m → search only that bucket → O(1) on average while the load factor stays bounded → resize by doubling keeps re-insertion O(1) amortized
Choose bucket = ⌊x / (t + 1)⌋ → two values in one bucket differ by at most t → any second arrival in a bucket is already an answer → each bucket holds at most one value
Values two or more buckets apart differ by at least t + 2 → only the own bucket and the two neighbours can hold a close value → three O(1) checks per step → Contains Duplicate III in O(n)
Keep only the last indexDiff values in the map (delete the one leaving) → index closeness is enforced by the window, value closeness by the buckets → O(min(n, indexDiff)) space
elevated: CPython uses open addressing and keeps the table at most 2/3 full → a colliding key probes other slots instead of chaining → resizes at 6, 11, 22, 43 keys, visible in sys.getsizeof
A hash is only as good as its spread → keys crafted to collide make lookups O(n) → Python salts string hashes per process
reference: hash(n) = n for small ints in CPython
the defaultdict placeholder-key detail in the source's version
a == b must imply hash(a) == hash(b); lists aren't hashable

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how a hash table finds a key in O(1), then how Contains Duplicate III reuses the idea with a bucket id you choose. Draw the number line cut into buckets of width 4 and mark which buckets you check for x = 5.
checklist: hash → bucket → search one bucket; load factor bounded by resizing
O(1) average, O(n) worst case under collisions
value bucket = x // (t + 1): same bucket guarantees |x − y| ≤ t
check own bucket and both neighbours; two buckets apart is always too far
window of the last indexDiff values, deleting the leaver each step

retrieve.q: Explain why a Python set lookup is called O(1) when two keys can land in the same bucket.
answer: the hash picks one bucket (slot); only its few colliding keys are compared
the table resizes to keep the load factor bounded (CPython ≤ 2/3), so collisions per lookup stay constant on average
worst case is O(n) if many keys collide

retrieve.q: Walk through step i = 4 of the trace (nums = [1, 5, 9, 1, 5, 9], indexDiff = 2, valueDiff = 3): which bucket does x land in, what is checked, and what leaves the window?
answer: own bucket 1 is empty (the earlier 5 left at i = 3)
store 5 in bucket 1, then delete 9 (from i = 2) as it leaves the window

retrieve.q: Why not keep a sorted window and binary-search for the nearest value? When is that the better choice?
answer: a sorted window gives O(log k) per step with a balanced tree, but Python has none built in and insort shifts O(k)
value buckets give O(1) per step with one dict
the sorted window is better when valueDiff changes per query or you need the closest pair, not just any close pair

compare.q: A dict of buckets vs using the array itself as a hash table: what does each use as the bucket id, and when does the array version win outright?
answer: dict: hash(key) or a chosen bucket function, any hashable keys
array-as-hash: the value itself is the index, so it needs small dense integers
the array has no collisions and no hashing cost
it fails for large, sparse or non-integer keys, where a dict is required

compare.q: Both cards slide a window and keep a dict. What does the dict hold in each, and why can this card delete exactly one entry per step while the counts window shrinks by several?
answer: here: bucket id → the one value in it; there: char → count still owed
this window has a fixed index length (indexDiff), so exactly one value leaves per step
the counts window's size varies: it shrinks while it stays valid, possibly many chars
both do O(1) dict work per pointer move, so both are O(n)

predict.q: Someone rewrites the bucket id as int(x / w) instead of x // w. With nums = [−2, 2], indexDiff = 1, valueDiff = 2, what does their version return, and what should it return?
predict.answer: It returns True, and the right answer is False. With w = 3, int(−2 / 3) = 0 and int(2 / 3) = 0, so −2 and 2 share bucket 0 and the second arrival is reported as close, though |2 − (−2)| = 4 > 2. Floor division puts −2 in bucket −1. Truncation toward zero makes bucket 0 twice as wide, so the guarantee that the same bucket means close no longer holds.

apply.task: Trace contains_near_dup([-3, 4, -1], 2, 2) by hand: write each value's bucket, the checks made, and the step where it returns. Then run the card's code with int(x / w) swapped in on [−2, 2], indexDiff 1, valueDiff 2, and compare with the correct version.
apply.done: Your trace gives buckets −1, 1, −1 (width 3) and returns True at i = 2 because −1 lands in −3's bucket (|−1 − (−3)| = 2). The truncating version returns True on [−2, 2] where the correct one returns False.
